passage:
12 November
Irfan forgot my birthday. Completely. No call, no message, nothing, and then he posted photos from a cricket match that evening. My first thought at 11 p.m. was: he never really cared. Classic Irfan, always about himself.
Then I made myself write the other list. Irfan drove three hours to help me move flats in the rain. He sat with me in the hospital when Papa had his operation. He lent me money without asking when I'd pay it back.
Both lists are true. He's caring and he's careless. Those aren't opposites; they're just two facts about one person. I don't have to erase the first list because of the second.
So tomorrow I'll call and tell him it stung. Not a verdict on our whole friendship, just one thing that hurt.
Abhinav

qa.q: What did Irfan post on the evening of the birthday?
qa.a: Photos from a cricket match.

qa.q: Why did 'he never really cared' feel true to Abhinav at 11 p.m.?
qa.a: The hurt of being forgotten was fresh and strong, so for that moment one careless act seemed to define the whole friendship.

qa.q: Which choice helped Abhinav keep the friendship steady?
qa.a: Writing the second list of Irfan's kindnesses and deciding to call about one thing that stung, instead of judging the whole friendship.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel when Abhinav calls tomorrow?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and sorry about forgetting, and relieved that Abhinav raised it as one hurt rather than ending things.

grounding: An adult hurt by a friend's forgotten birthday reminds themselves that the friend is both caring and careless, and plans a calm conversation instead of a verdict.

passage:
Afreen: my manager presented my report to the directors today. didn't mention my name once 😠
Jagdish: WHAT. after you stayed till 11 all week??
Afreen: yes. i was ready to write her off completely. like she's just a credit-stealer, always has been
Jagdish: is she though?
Afreen: ugh. no. she's the one who fought for my leave when Abba was in hospital. she trained me for months
Afreen: so i'm trying to hold both. she's generous AND she was careless today
Jagdish: that's very grown up of you 🙂
Afreen: it's very annoying of me. but if i decide she's a villain i'll be miserable at work for a year
Jagdish: fair. so what now?
Afreen: i'll tell her tomorrow, calmly, that i'd like my name on the slides next time
Jagdish: and if she's weird about it?
Afreen: then that's a third fact. i'll deal with it 🙏

qa.q: Who presented Afreen's report to the directors?
qa.a: Afreen's manager.

qa.q: Why was Afreen ready to 'write her off completely'?
qa.a: Afreen felt angry and unseen after staying late all week, and in that moment the credit-taking seemed to be all the manager was.

qa.q: What choice did Afreen make about tomorrow, and why is it a steady one?
qa.a: To ask the manager calmly for Afreen's name on the slides next time, which raises the real problem without turning a generous person into a villain.

qa.q: How might the manager react to Afreen's calm request?
qa.a: She may feel embarrassed about the oversight and, given her past support, will likely fix it; being asked calmly makes that easier.

grounding: In a chat an adult angry at a manager who took credit is reminded by their own memories that the manager is both generous and careless, and plans a calm request.

passage:
In the kasba of Nabha, Kiran and Salma ran a small tailoring shop together above the sweet shop. On Monday morning Kiran found the door unlocked and two bolts of wedding silk gone. Salma had forgotten to lock up again.
Kiran's first thought, standing in the empty doorway, was hot and total: she's useless, she's always been careless, I should never have trusted her. Then she sat on the step and made herself remember. Salma had sat up three nights with Kiran's baby during the fever. Salma had taught her to cut blouse patterns for nothing. Salma was kind, and Salma was careless. Both.
When Salma arrived, pale, Kiran said, "I'm very angry about the silk. I'm not angry about you. From now on, I lock up." Salma cried, and then they walked to the police station together.

qa.q: What was missing from the shop on Monday morning?
qa.a: Two bolts of wedding silk.

qa.q: Why did 'she's useless' feel so true to Kiran in the doorway?
qa.a: The loss was sudden and costly, so her anger made one careless act feel like the whole truth about Salma.

qa.q: Which choice helped Kiran respond without breaking the partnership?
qa.a: Remembering Salma's kindness on the step, then separating her anger about the silk from her view of Salma, and taking over the locking up herself.

qa.q: What might Salma have feared as she arrived at the shop?
qa.a: That Kiran would end their partnership or friendship; hearing 'I'm not angry about you' likely brought huge relief along with guilt.

grounding: A woman whose business partner's carelessness cost them stock reminds herself the partner is also deeply kind, and responds without an explosion.

passage:
The last train into Porto arrived at midnight, and Tariq had promised to pick Rosa up. She stood under the station awning for forty minutes, rain dripping off the edge, calling a phone that went to voicemail.
In the taxi home the old voice started: He doesn't care. He never did. She caught it. That wasn't true either. In March, Tariq had sat with her in the emergency room for six hours when she broke her wrist. He'd learned to make her grandmother's soup.
Rosa said it to herself slowly, like a sum: Tariq is caring. Tariq was careless tonight. Both are real.
In the morning he appeared at her door, grey-faced. "I fell asleep on the sofa. I'm so sorry."
"I was really upset," Rosa said. "I still am, a bit. And I know you care. Can you set an alarm next time?"
He nodded, and they made coffee.

qa.q: How long did Rosa wait under the station awning?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did "He doesn't care. He never did" feel true to Rosa in the taxi?
qa.a: She was cold, tired and hurt after waiting in the rain, and in that disappointment one careless night seemed to wipe out everything good.

qa.q: What choice in the taxi kept the disappointment from exploding?
qa.a: Rosa remembered the emergency room and the soup and held both facts, caring and careless, so she could say she was upset and ask for an alarm without calling the friendship a lie.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tariq to hear "And I know you care"?
qa.a: Tariq, grey-faced and ashamed, would probably feel relieved that the mistake was named honestly without being treated as proof that he didn't care.

grounding: Shows an adult who, after being let down, tells herself a friend is both caring and careless, which keeps her disappointment honest but steady.

passage:
In the staffroom of the Pune school where they both taught Class 7, Zainab found out at eight: the unit-test marks she'd handed Aditi to upload had never reached the office. The principal wanted to know why Zainab's section had no marks.
Her first thought was sharp: Aditi always does this. Only helps when it suits. Then Zainab looked at the grey cardigan on her own chair, Aditi's cardigan, lent last week when Zainab had fever and Aditi had quietly taken her classes for two days.
Both, she told herself. Aditi is generous, and Aditi is disorganised. One doesn't cancel the other.
At break she said, "Aditi, the marks didn't go in, and the principal questioned me. That was stressful."
Aditi's hand flew to cover a gasp. "Oh no. It's still on my pen drive."
"Can you send it now? And let's keep a checklist for uploads."
The marks went in by lunch. The cardigan went back with a thank-you note.

qa.q: What had Aditi lent Zainab last week?
qa.a: Aditi's grey cardigan, when Zainab had fever.

qa.q: Why did "Aditi always does this" come to Zainab's mind first?
qa.a: Being questioned by the principal made her anxious and stung, and in that moment one careless mistake seemed to define Aditi completely.

qa.q: How did holding both facts shape what Zainab said at break?
qa.a: She named the problem and the stress plainly without attacking Aditi's character, then asked for the file and a checklist, which fixed things by lunch.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel being told calmly instead of blamed?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt embarrassed but safe enough to own the mistake straight away, instead of getting defensive.

grounding: Illustrates an adult who keeps in view that a colleague is both generous and careless, so a mistake leads to a calm fix rather than an explosion.
